title: Review TermAl tests for aggressive wall-clock assertions; separate real product requirements from fragile timing assumptions and fix the fragile ones
outcome: TermAl's tests don't fail because of scheduling or load: each wall-clock assertion left in place rests on a named real requirement, and the fragile ones are replaced by checks that still catch the regression they were written for.
acceptance: A census lists the wall-clock, elapsed-time, deadline and budget assertions in TermAl's Rust and UI tests and in scripts, each classified as a real product requirement with its source, a fragile assumption, or a harmless guard such as a deadlock bound, and gives what regression each was meant to catch

Each fragile assertion that has failed or that the census ranks high is replaced by a check that doesn't depend on the host's scheduler or, where a limit only detects a hang, by waiting on the condition under a long hang-detecting limit, per Greg's ruling of 2026-11-04; no retry, quarantine or raised limit is used to hide a failure whose cause is unknown; each carries a recorded failing run against the regression it protects where such a regression can be produced, or a stated reason; and the 50 ms gate in state_lock_parallel.rs is left to Greg.
Any failures seen tonight on DL560 or Windows B that turn out to be timing are classified here, with their run ids
Greg gets the results and priorities; no stored evaluation is changed
